title: Chunking, Embeddings and Indexes
tagline: The content is in, but in pieces. Cut it, embed it and index it so the right piece can be found.
story: Parsed text is still one long stream, and a model cannot read a thousand pages for each question. The system must cut the text into retrievable pieces, turn each piece into a vector, and store the vectors where a filtered nearest-neighbour search can find them in milliseconds. Every choice here is a trade: a chunk too small loses its meaning, a vector too large exhausts memory, and a filter too selective can return nothing. This world is the choice of chunk, model, compression and index, and the discipline of measuring each against your own questions.
oneLiner: Choose how to cut, embed, compress and index content, and prove each choice on your own questions.
youWillLearn: Pick a chunking strategy by document shape and query type, and size overlap and index inflation
Restore context to small chunks with headers, parent-child retrieval, contextual retrieval, late chunking, propositions and RAPTOR, and know the ingest cost of each
Represent tables, code and figures so they stay answerable
Choose an embedding model, dimensions, Matryoshka truncation and quantization from a memory and recall budget
Apply asymmetric prompts, and plan for model drift and retirement
Compare flat, HNSW, IVF and DiskANN, tune m, efConstruction and efSearch, and explain why filters collapse recall
Pick a vector store by scale, filters, data gravity and operations model

flashcards.front: What is Microsoft's suggested starting point for chunking, and how should you treat it?
flashcards.back: 512 tokens (about 2,000 characters) with 25% overlap (128 tokens). It is a starting point to test on your own questions, not a rule.

flashcards.front: What is the Text Split skill default `maximumPageLength` and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: 5,000 characters (range 300 to 50,000), about 1,250 tokens, well above the 512-token advice. Set it on purpose, with `pageOverlapLength` if you want overlap.

flashcards.front: What is the catch with Text Split token mode?
flashcards.back: `unit: azureOpenAITokens` is preview. The tokenizer defaults to `cl100k_base`, and `o200k_base` (GPT-4o) is not supported, so counts can differ from the model's.

flashcards.front: What does chunk size research say about question type?
flashcards.back: One multi-dataset study found 64 to 128 tokens best for short factual answers and 512 to 1,024 for broader context. NVIDIA found 128 and 2,048 generally weaker. Test on your queries.

flashcards.front: Is semantic chunking worth its compute?
flashcards.back: A 2024 study found its extra compute was not justified by consistent gains over fixed-size chunking. Compare it with a recursive baseline on your own questions first.

flashcards.front: How much does 25% overlap inflate the chunk count?
flashcards.back: 512-token chunks with 128 overlap step by 384 tokens, so about 33% more chunks than no overlap, plus repeated tokens in prompts. Unstructured defaults to overlap 0.

flashcards.front: What did Contextual Retrieval measure?
flashcards.back: Top-20 failure rate fell 35% with contextual embeddings (5.7% to 3.7%), 49% adding contextual BM25 (2.9%) and 67% adding reranking (1.9%). It is a vendor study.

flashcards.front: What is the Contextual Retrieval cost estimate and its assumptions?
flashcards.back: About 1.02 dollars per million document tokens, one time, with prompt caching, assuming 800-token chunks, 8k-token documents and 100 tokens of context per chunk.

flashcards.front: What does late chunking need, and what does it change?
flashcards.back: A long-context embedding model (jina-embeddings-v2-base-en takes 8,192 tokens). It embeds the whole text first and mean-pools per chunk, so each vector carries document context.

flashcards.front: How does Azure AI Search do parent-child retrieval?
flashcards.back: Index projections write one index document per child chunk with a `parent_id`. `projectionMode` `skipIndexingParentDocuments` is recommended. Child keys carry a hash that changes with the parent.

flashcards.front: What do propositions and RAPTOR each cost?
flashcards.back: Propositions need an LLM pass at ingest and many more vectors. RAPTOR needs summarisation calls and a rebuild of affected subtrees when documents change.

flashcards.front: What are the text-embedding-3 default dimensions, and what does `dimensions` do?
flashcards.back: 1,536 (small) and 3,072 (large). `dimensions` shortens the vector. If you truncate by hand, re-normalise. A 256-dimension 3-large vector beat full ada-002 on MTEB.

flashcards.front: Why does MIRACL matter more than the MTEB average when choosing 3-small or 3-large?
flashcards.back: MTEB averages are 62.3 and 64.6, a small gap. MIRACL multilingual retrieval averages are 44.0 and 54.9 (ada-002 31.4), a large one. Test your own languages.

flashcards.front: What limits Matryoshka truncation in Azure AI Search?
flashcards.back: `truncationDimension` needs scalar or binary quantization, HNSW and `Edm.Half` or `Edm.Single` fields. It cannot be added to an existing field and has no portal support.

flashcards.front: What do scalar and binary quantization save, and what do they keep?
flashcards.back: int8 is 4 times smaller and keeps about 99.3% of performance in an open benchmark. Binary is 32 times smaller (AI Search says up to 28) and keeps about 96% with rescoring.

flashcards.front: What are oversampling and rescoring in AI Search?
flashcards.back: Fetch `defaultOversampling` times more candidates (default 4) from the compressed vectors, then rescore with the originals. Rescoring works only with HNSW.

flashcards.front: Why do query and document prefixes matter?
flashcards.back: E5 needs `query: ` and `passage: `. BGE v1.5 adds an instruction to queries only. Nomic uses `search_query: ` and `search_document: `. Missing prefixes silently lower quality.

flashcards.front: What are the HNSW defaults in Azure AI Search and pgvector?
flashcards.back: AI Search: `m` 4, `efConstruction` 400, `efSearch` 500. pgvector: `m` 16, `ef_construction` 64, `hnsw.ef_search` 40. Higher values buy recall with memory, build time or latency.

flashcards.front: Name the AI Search vector filter modes.
flashcards.back: `preFilter` (default for newer indexes, best recall), `postFilter` (may miss results) and `strictPostFilter` (preview, may return zero). Consider `exhaustive: true` for very selective filters.

flashcards.front: Why can a filtered pgvector HNSW query return too few rows?
flashcards.back: It filters after the approximate scan. With `ef_search` 40 and a filter matching 10% of rows, you get about 4 rows. Iterative scans (0.8.0+) or partial indexes fix it.

flashcards.front: What are the Cosmos DB for NoSQL vector index types?
flashcards.back: `flat` (exact, up to 505 dimensions), `quantizedFlat` and `diskANN` (up to 4,096). Approximate types need at least 1,000 vectors, and policies cannot be edited in place.

flashcards.front: How much memory do raw vectors need?
flashcards.back: vectors x dimensions x 4 bytes for float32: one million at 1,536 dimensions is about 6.1 GB. HNSW adds 1% to 20%, and AI Search treats the vector quota as a memory quota.

glossary.def: The unit of text you embed, index and retrieve. It is also the unit you paste into the prompt unless you expand to a parent.
Tokens shared by neighbouring chunks so a fact on a boundary is not cut in two. It raises the chunk count and repeats tokens in prompts.
Cut on the largest separator that keeps chunks under the size limit (sections, paragraphs, lines, sentences, words), falling back to smaller ones.
Match small child chunks for precision, then return the larger parent for context. Also called small-to-big.
Prepend a short LLM-written context sentence to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing, so a chunk says what it is about.
Embed the whole document with a long-context model, then pool token embeddings per chunk so each vector carries document context.
An atomic, self-contained statement of fact extracted from a passage, used as the retrieval unit (Dense X Retrieval).
A fixed-length vector from a model that places similar meanings near each other, compared by cosine, dot product or Euclidean distance.
An embedding trained so its leading dimensions form a usable shorter vector. Truncating a non-Matryoshka vector is not safe.
Store each dimension as an 8-bit integer instead of a 32-bit float, for 4 times less memory with a small recall loss.
Store one bit per dimension. It saves up to 28 to 32 times the memory and relies on oversampling and rescoring to recover recall.
Fetch more candidates than needed from compressed vectors, then re-rank them with full-precision vectors.
Hierarchical navigable small world: a layered proximity graph walked greedily from the top. Tuned by `m`, `efConstruction` and `efSearch`.
Inverted file index: cluster vectors into lists and search only the nearest lists (`probes`). Often combined with product quantization.
A graph index designed to live mostly on SSD, so billion-point sets fit on a single node with limited RAM.
Apply the metadata filter during the vector search so the result set is made only of matching items, at some latency cost.
Compare the query with every vector for exact results. Right for small or highly filtered candidate sets.

claims.text: Microsoft's chunking guide suggests starting at 512 tokens (about 2,000 characters) with 25% overlap (128 tokens), and also shows a fixed-size example of about 600 characters with 10 to 15% overlap.

The Text Split skill has maximumPageLength default 5,000 characters (300 to 50,000), pageOverlapLength with no overlap by default, unit characters or azureOpenAITokens (preview), a default tokenizer of cl100k_base, and does not support o200k_base.
A multi-dataset fixed-size study found 64 to 128 token chunks best for short fact-based answers and 512 to 1,024 token chunks better when broader context is needed.
NVIDIA found page-level chunking had the best average accuracy (0.648) with the lowest standard deviation (0.107), and that 128 and 2,048 token chunks generally underperformed.
A 2024 study across retrieval and answer generation found the extra compute of semantic chunking was not justified by consistent gains over fixed-size chunking.
Unstructured open-source chunking defaults to max_characters 500 and overlap 0.
Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 35% (5.7% to 3.7%) with contextual embeddings, by 49% (to 2.9%) adding contextual BM25 and by 67% (to 1.9%) adding reranking.

Anthropic estimated a one-time cost of 1.02 dollars per million document tokens for contextual retrieval with prompt caching, assuming 800 token chunks, 8k token documents, 50 token instructions and 100 tokens of context per chunk.
Late chunking embeds the whole text first and mean-pools token embeddings per chunk, and needs a long-context embedding model such as jina-embeddings-v2-base-en, which handles 8,192 tokens.
With GPT-4, RAPTOR raised the best QuALITY result by 20% absolute accuracy.

In Azure AI Search index projections the parent id field must be Edm.String and filterable and not the document key, projectionMode skipIndexingParentDocuments is recommended, projected keys contain a hash that changes when the parent changes, and child chunks of a deleted parent are removed only if the data source has a deletion detection policy.

text-embedding-3-small and -large default to 1,536 and 3,072 dimensions, have MTEB averages of 62.3 and 64.6 (ada-002 61.0), a 256-dimension 3-large vector beat full-size ada-002 on MTEB, and a vector truncated by hand should be re-normalised.

The Azure embedding model table lists MIRACL averages of 31.4 (ada-002), 44.0 (3-small) and 54.9 (3-large), up to 2,048 input items per call, and says you cannot upgrade in place between embedding models.
The Azure OpenAI retirement schedule page (updated 2026-09-21) lists text-embedding-3-large, text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-ada-002 as retiring on 2028-02-09.
Cohere embed-v4.0 supports output dimensions 256, 512, 1,024 or 1,536 (default) with a 128k context, and embed-v5.0-pro and embed-v5.0-fast default to 2,048 dimensions.
E5 requires the prefixes query: and passage:, BGE v1.5 adds an instruction to queries only, and missing prefixes silently lower quality.
MTEB v1 covers 8 task types and 58 datasets and no single method won every task.

In Azure AI Search truncationDimension works only with scalar or binary quantization, HNSW and Edm.Half or Edm.Single fields, cannot be added to an existing field, and with stored false a partial update loses vectors unless the full vector is resent.

In Azure AI Search scalar quantization is int8 (4 times smaller) and binary is 1 bit per dimension (up to 28 times smaller, best above 1,024 dimensions), rescoring works only with HNSW, defaultOversampling defaults to 4, discardOriginals is binary only, and quantization needs a new vector profile and field.

A Hugging Face experiment found int8 quantization gives 4 times less memory with about 99.3% of float32 performance, and binary gives 32 times less memory keeping about 96% with rescoring and about 92.5% without.
In Azure AI Search the vector index size quota is a memory quota, and HNSW adds 1% to 20% overhead on top of float32 vectors.
Azure AI Search HNSW defaults are m 4 (range 4 to 10), efConstruction 400 (100 to 1,000) and efSearch 500 (100 to 1,000).

pgvector HNSW defaults are m 16, ef_construction 64 and hnsw.ef_search 40, a filter matching 10% of rows with ef_search 40 returns about 4 rows, IVFFlat probes defaults to 1, and iterative scans arrived in 0.8.0 with hnsw.max_scan_tuples defaulting to 20,000.
Qdrant defaults to HNSW m 16 and ef_construct 100, and payload indexes should be created before ingest so the graph gets filter-aware edges.
Azure AI Search vectorFilterMode offers preFilter, postFilter and strictPostFilter (preview), and indexes created before about 2023-10-15 default to postFilter.

Cosmos DB for NoSQL vector indexes are flat (up to 505 dimensions), quantizedFlat and diskANN (up to 4,096), the last two need at least 1,000 vectors or a full scan runs, and vector policies cannot be edited in place.
The DiskANN paper indexes, stores and searches a billion-point database on a single workstation with 64 GB of RAM and an SSD.
Pinecone serverless indexes allow from 100 namespaces (Starter) to 1,000,000 (Enterprise), and one namespace per tenant is its documented multitenancy pattern.
